title: Why an extension doesn't extend payment: IRS rules accountants need on Mac, 2026
metaTitle: Extension doesn't extend payment: IRS guide for accountants
description: An extension to file is not an extension to pay. Learn the IRS payment deadline, penalty math and free fixes for accountants and their clients.
secondaryKeywords: extension to file vs extension to pay
intro: An extension doesn't extend payment. Form 4868 gives you more time to file the return, usually until mid-October. The tax you owe is still due on the original date, usually April 15, and penalties start counting from that day. This page covers what the mistake costs, why it keeps happening, and the fixes you can use this week without buying anything.
tldr: Form 4868 extends the time to file. It does not extend the time to pay.
Unpaid tax carries a failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% per month, capped at 25%, counted from the original due date.
Pay your estimate by the original due date with IRS Direct Pay, using the Extension reason.
If you cannot pay, an IRS payment plan costs $0 to $69 to set up, and penalties and interest continue.

blocks.text: Start with the sentence that settles it. An extension to file is not an extension to pay. The IRS says this in plain words on Topic 304: an extension of time to file is not an extension of time to pay. If your client owes tax, the money is due on the original date.
Two deadlines, one return

Think of one return with two clocks. The filing clock is the deadline for sending the return. Form 4868 moves that clock to mid-October. The payment clock starts at the original due date and does not move when you file the extension. Most confusion happens because people assume one clock controls both.

rows: Time to send in your return

blocks.text: The IRS Direct Pay help page says the same thing from another angle. It states that a filing extension does not extend the deadline to pay what you owe. Read that line twice before you advise a client. Then check how your intake form and tax software describe the extension.
What the mistake costs your clients

The main cost is the failure-to-pay penalty. The IRS charges 0.5% of unpaid tax for each month or part of a month. The penalty is capped at 25% of unpaid tax. A partial month counts in full, so a payment one day into a new month triggers the full 0.5%.

blocks.caption: Example for one client. Interest is not included.

blocks.text: The table leaves out interest. Interest also runs from the original due date. It does not stop when a payment plan starts. Penalties and interest both begin on the original due date, even when the return is filed on time.
A worked example for one client

Take a client who owes $8,400 in federal tax. The return is due April 15. The client files Form 4868 and pays nothing by that date. Here is what the penalty looks like at three moments, using the 0.5% monthly rate.

items: Paid by April 15: no failure-to-pay penalty applies. Interest is not part of this example.
Paid on June 20: that is the third month after April 15, so the penalty is 1.5%, or $126.
Paid in mid-October: that is six months, so the penalty is 3%, or $252. Clients who wait for the extended date pay the most.
On a timely filer's approved payment plan, the rate drops to 0.25% per month, or $21 a month on $8,400.

blocks.text: Run the same numbers on your own client files. Change the balance and the months, and the cost becomes clear. A $300 balance at 0.5% per month adds $1.50 a month. Small amounts matter less to the bill than to the client's trust.
Build a tracker in Excel that flags the gap early

A tracker catches the gap before the IRS does. Open a new workbook in Excel for Microsoft 365. Put one client on each row. Use these columns: Client in A, Original due date in B, Estimated tax owed in C, and Amount paid in D.

Then add two formulas. In E2, type =C2-D2 for the balance still owed. In F2, type =B2-TODAY() for the days left before the original due date. Fill both down with the Fill handle. A negative number in F means the date has already passed.

Flag the risk with Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Less Than, then enter 30. Apply the rule to column F so rows with fewer than 30 days left stand out. Sort by balance once a week so the largest bills get the first call.
For more checks on formulas and month-end work, see [Excel help for accountants on Mac](/for/accountants/excel).
Payment plans when the client cannot pay in full

An IRS payment plan can help when cash is short. The online application covers a simple installment agreement for $50,000 or less in combined tax, penalties and interest. A short-term plan of 180 days or less covers balances under $100,000.

Setup fees depend on the plan. A pay-in-full or short-term plan costs $0. A long-term plan costs $29 with direct debit, waived for low income, or $69 without direct debit, or $43 for low income. Penalties and interest continue during the plan.

A plan is not a way to skip the first payment. Pay as much as you can by the original due date, then set up the plan for the rest. Every dollar paid early stops the penalty from growing on that dollar.
Mistakes accountants make with extensions

items: Telling a client the extension covers the tax bill. It covers only the filing date.
Filing the extension and assuming the payment can wait until October.
Estimating the balance too low, then paying the rest months later with penalties on top.
Sending a reminder by phone only. Put the payment date in writing too.
Skipping state rules. State extension and payment rules differ from federal rules.
Pasting client balances into a chat tool before checking your firm's rules on client data.

blocks.text: A reminder email you can send this week

Here is a short draft. Subject: Your tax payment is due April 15, even with an extension. Body: We filed an extension for your return, which moves the filing date to mid-October. It does not move the payment date. Please pay your estimated balance by April 15 through IRS Direct Pay, using the Extension reason. We will confirm the final amount once the return is complete.
Check the dates for your tax year before you send it. Use ⌘N in Outlook to start a new message. Keep client names and balances out of any AI tool unless your firm allows it.
What helps clients act on time

Reminder wording matters. UK field experiments with more than 200,000 people found that social-norm and public-goods messages in standard tax reminder letters considerably raised compliance. Those messages cost nothing to add. The study covers general tax, not accountant clients, so test the wording on your own letters.
Put the payment date first in the subject line. Add one line about the extension after it. Send one reminder about two weeks before the date, and one on the date itself.
Where Lazur fits, and where it does not

Lazur does not file, pay or click for you. It is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about what is on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur circles it. Ask how to do a step, and Lazur guides you one click at a time.

For client files, check your firm's rules first. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Regulated work still needs your employer's approval before client data goes on screen.
What to do this week

Pick the one client with the largest balance and the earliest date. Make that call first. Then build the tracker for the rest of the list. Work from the biggest risk down, and you will catch most of the gaps before the penalty starts to grow.

faq.question: Does filing an extension give my client more time to pay?
faq.answer: No. An extension of time to file is not an extension of time to pay. The payment is still due on the original date, usually April 15. Penalties and interest start from that date.

faq.question: Do I still need Form 4868 if the client pays through Direct Pay?
faq.answer: Not if the payment succeeds. IRS Direct Pay help says that when you select Extension as the reason and the Apply Payment to field begins with 4868, a successful payment grants the extension automatically.

faq.question: What is the penalty on $8,400 unpaid for three months?
faq.answer: The failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% per month. Three months is 1.5%, or $126. Interest is extra. This is a worked example for one client, not a quote.

faq.question: Does a payment plan stop the penalty?
faq.answer: Not completely. Penalties and interest continue on a payment plan. For timely filers on an approved plan, the penalty rate drops to 0.25% per month.

faq.question: What does an IRS payment plan cost to set up?
faq.answer: A pay-in-full or short-term plan has a $0 setup fee. A long-term plan costs $29 with direct debit, waived for low income, or $69 without direct debit, or $43 for low income.

faq.question: Can Lazur pay the IRS or check a client balance for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It points, guides, answers out loud and drafts text. You make the payment yourself.

faq.question: Does this advice cover state taxes?
faq.answer: No. This page covers federal rules only. State extension and payment rules differ. Check the tax agency for the state where your client files.

costs.title: Penalties that start on the original date
costs.text: The failure-to-pay penalty runs from the original due date, not the extended one. The IRS charges 0.5% of unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, capped at 25% of the unpaid tax. A timely filer on an approved payment plan pays 0.25% per month instead. Each month adds to the bill, and the extension does not pause it.

costs.title: Interest on top of the penalty
costs.text: Interest runs alongside the penalty on the unpaid balance. This page does not quote the interest rate, so check the current figure on irs.gov before you give a client a number. A payment plan does not stop interest either. Clients often watch the penalty and forget the interest.

costs.title: Repeat calls and rework
costs.text: A client who misreads the deadline calls near the due date, asks for the same explanation twice and sometimes files late anyway. Each call takes time you could spend on other returns. A September 2026 NATP survey, reported in a secondhand summary, said 90% of respondents called client misunderstandings about extensions common.

costs.title: Your busy season hours
costs.text: A 2026 Distinct survey of tax and audit professionals found that 78% worked more than 50 hours a week in busy season. The survey did not state its sample size, and its author is a recruitment firm, so treat the figure as a signal. BLS also notes longer work periods during tax season. Extra payment calls land in the same weeks you have the least time.

causes.title: Extension sounds like relief
causes.text: The word extension suggests that everything gets pushed back. In everyday speech, an extension means more time for anything. A client who hears that the return is extended may assume the bill is extended too. The word is accurate for the return and misleading for the money.

causes.title: The form points at filing
causes.text: Form 4868 is an application for more time to file your return, and its title says so. Many people still see a form, an extension and a payment in the same conversation. Those three ideas blur together. The paperwork does not separate the two clocks for them.

causes.title: Clients hear it from other people
causes.text: Clients often get tax information from friends, forums and quick web searches. A September 2026 NATP survey summary said 48% of respondents believed clients think an extension gives more time to pay. Another 23% said clients assume penalties and interest do not apply after an extension. Those beliefs travel faster than careful IRS wording.

causes.title: IRS wording is accurate but dense
causes.text: The IRS says a filing extension does not extend the deadline to pay what you owe. That sentence is clear once you read it. It sits inside a long help page, though, next to fields and deadlines. A busy reader skims past it and keeps the older belief.

causes.title: Busy season squeezes the explanation
causes.text: When dozens of returns are open, the deadline talk is brief. A one-line explanation at intake is often skipped. The confusion costs the most in busy season, because clients call late and the due date is close. The Distinct survey found heavy weekly hours across public accounting in 2026.

causes.title: State rules differ
causes.text: Each state sets its own extension and payment rules. This page covers federal rules only, and it did not research state deadlines or penalties. A client who owes state tax may face a different date. Check the state tax agency before you give advice that covers both.

fixes.title: Pay by the original due date with the Extension reason
fixes.text: Use IRS Direct Pay between January 1 and the original due date. Select Extension as the Reason for Payment. Make sure the Apply Payment to field begins with 4868. If the payment succeeds, the extension is granted automatically, and no separate Form 4868 is needed. Keep the confirmation page in the client file.

fixes.title: Pay the estimate you can support
fixes.text: Penalties apply to unpaid tax. Paying most of the estimated balance by the original date shrinks the base the penalty uses. Pay what you can estimate with reasonable confidence, then true up when the return is final. A partial payment still stops the penalty on the amount paid.

fixes.title: Set an installment plan early
fixes.text: If the cash is not there, apply for an IRS payment plan rather than waiting. A simple installment agreement covers combined tax, penalties and interest of $50,000 or less. A short-term plan of 180 days or less covers balances under $100,000. The setup fee is $0 for pay-in-full or short-term plans.

fixes.title: Set two alarms in Reminders
fixes.text: Open Reminders on your Mac. Press ⌘N to make a new reminder. Set one alert about two weeks before the original due date and one on the due date. Some Reminders features need updated iCloud reminders, so check the account type first. Apple's Reminders guide covers the setup.

fixes.title: Put the payment date in every letter
fixes.text: Write the original due date in the first line of every client letter, and the extension date second. Use the same two dates in the email, the tracker and the call script. Consistent wording is easier for a client to repeat to a spouse or a bookkeeper.

fixes.title: Try a social-norm line in reminders
fixes.text: A UK study of more than 200,000 people found that social-norm messages in standard tax reminder letters raised compliance, at no cost to add. Wording of that kind may help your letters. Test it on a small batch first, because the study covers general tax letters, not accountant clients.

fixes.title: Check the state rule before you advise
fixes.text: Look up the tax agency for the client's state. Check the extension rule, the payment date and the penalty rate. Write the state answer in the same tracker as the federal answer, so the client gets one set of dates.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the tracker
plan.text: Open Excel and create columns for client, original due date, estimated tax owed, amount paid, balance and days left. Add the two formulas in row 2 and fill them down. Enter every open client, even the ones you think are fine.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Sort by date and balance
plan.text: Sort the tracker by days left, then by balance. Mark clients with a balance above zero and fewer than 30 days left. Those are your first calls. Note which clients have already paid through Direct Pay.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Send the reminder
plan.text: Draft one reminder in Outlook with the payment date first. Send it to the clients on the flagged list. Keep a copy in the client file, following your firm's rules on client data.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Read the payment steps
plan.text: Open the IRS Direct Pay help page and read the Extension reason steps. Note the three fields you will use. Do not submit a test payment. Bookmark the page in Chrome with ⌘D so you can return to it quickly.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set the alarms
plan.text: Create two Reminders alerts for each flagged client, one about two weeks before the original due date and one on that date. Review the tracker every Friday until the date passes.
